title: The future, and what might have been
version: Published online 30 January 2018; Philosophical Studies 176 (2019), 505–532; DOI 10.1007/s11098-017-1026-y
locator: Publisher full-text HTML, selected: §1 (publisher lines 64–72), §1.1 (lines 73–110), §2 (lines 111–124), §2.1 (lines 125–165), §2.2 (lines 188–192); locators are section numbers because publisher HTML has no stable pagination for individual passages.
assumptions: Growing-block ontology; abstract ersatz timelines; feasible extensions share history and laws; selected supervaluational semantics for future claims; primitive non-Humean laws/lawmakers.
conclusion: Authors propose that past and present concrete things plus laws make future truths true; candidate lawmakers are left open but must constrain block growth. Feasible histories may diverge despite sharing present history and laws, making some future sentences indeterminate under their selected semantics.
proof_status: Conceptual framework selectively inspected; no formal proof audit or physical model reproduction.
dependencies: Briggs and Forbes, The Real Truth about the Unreal Future (2012), p. 298 as summarized/cited in §1.1
open_questions: What exact facts individuate lawmakers, and do equal classical causal-past field data fix them?
Can the feasible extension structure be supplied by a specified relativistic field model without adding a preferred global present?
relevance: Strong law-based growing-block rival directly tests whether future truth requires existing future events and whether same past fixes complete grounds.
limits: Selected sections only, not a complete audit. Authors explicitly do not defend growing block in this paper and say they do not provide a complete theory of each nomological-package element. No relativistic causal-past formalization or theorem equating past data with lawmakers. The 2012 source was not re-read; its publisher abstract remains the only source checked for it.
